summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, hypertension, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for acute worsening dyspnea that began suddenly while eating. She reported a 22-pound weight gain over the prior two months and had not resumed her diuretic medication after a recent hospitalization for heart failure. Initial evaluation revealed moderate pulmonary edema on chest X-ray, elevated proBNP, and clinical signs of fluid overload. Her heart function was preserved with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 71%, consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). She was treated with intravenous diuresis, transitioned to oral torsemide and spironolactone, and had improvement in symptoms and fluid status. A pMIBI scan showed normal perfusion and no ischemia. Urine culture grew E. coli and Klebsiella but was asymptomatic and not treated. She was discharged to extended care for rehabilitation with a plan for strict weight monitoring and medication adherence.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris
Decreased white blood cell count, unspecified

Family history of ischemic heart disease and other diseases of the circulatory system
